steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on the Acoustic Soft Tactile skin (AST), a low-cost stand-alone soft tactile sensor based on acoustics. Motivate it from the limits of current soft tactile sensors, review prior acoustic tactile sensing work, and finish with our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Limitations of current soft tactile sensors
2. Why tactile sensing matters; transduction methods for soft sensors
3. Acoustic sensing in a soft pneumatic finger
4. Other acoustic tactile sensors
5. Design lessons and our AST
6. Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Limitations
- persistent limitations despite advances (recent review on tactile sensing technologies)
- commercial soft sensors: fixed shapes/sizes -> hard to integrate, esp. space-constrained
- camera-based sensors: space requirements
- intricate electrical components in tight spaces -> sophisticated manufacturing, high cost
- need: less complex sensing, adapts to shapes, limited space, form factors

2. Tactile sensing in robotics
- accurate measurement of physical interaction: human-robot interaction, grasping, manipulation
- tactile sensing observes interaction state
- tactile predictive models -> predictive controller (slippage control, cluster manipulation) -> safer, more precise, efficient
- soft sensors: deformable objects, robust manipulation; soft flexible surface, deformation gives normal/shear forces, contact location, texture
- electronic: resistive, capacitive, piezoelectric, magnetic, impedance
- non-electronic: camera-based, fluid-based, acoustics; combinations

3. Zoller et al.
- sound waves in pneumatically actuated soft finger; speaker + microphone in actuation chamber
- microphone monitors sound modulation; amplitude changes when finger deforms under external force
- measured contact forces and contact location with certain precision
- but integrated with finger, not stand-alone for other robot counterparts

4. Acoustic tactile sensors
- tactile features: contacts, deformations, forces, shape recognition
- Shinoda et al.: silicone hemispherical fingertip, ultrasound transmitter/receiver array; deformations up to 10µm, inclination changes to 0.001 radians; later hollow cavity, stress via acoustic resonance
- Teramoto et al.: flexible membrane over acoustic transducers, object curvature
- Tanaka et al.: real-time lump detection in laparoscopic surgery, silicone hollow tube
- Chuang et al.: ultrasonic, static normal force (1-6 N), shape recognition, time-of-flight; TFT layer between piezoelectric PVDF layers + soft polymer surface -> sophisticated manufacturing

5. Lessons + AST
- V. Wall et al.: force location + material characteristics, soft pneumatic finger, enclosed speaker + microphone ("revolution")
- microphone only: still forces, locations, materials, but needs sound generated at contact point
- potential of acoustics for soft deformation
- low-cost skin: (1) no complex circuitry in skin, (2) sensory hardware away from surface -> compact, no sophisticated manufacturing, many form factors
- AST: low-cost, easily manufacturable standalone sensor

6. Contributions
- stand-alone, low-cost, different shapes and sizes (Fig. 1 a)
- (i) open-source low-cost sensor, easy to fabricate; key parts: membrane with embedded acoustic channels, microphone, speakers
- (ii) frame-less AST (f-AST) for non-flat surfaces
- (iii) regression and classification methods: force + location vs microphone readings
- (iv) robotic tasks: flat and non-flat surface, force-controlled pick-and-place -> realistic applications

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Soft tactile sensing has made progress, but it still has persistent limitations, as a recent review on tactile sensing technologies discusses. A lot of the soft tactile sensors that are commercially available have fixed shapes and sizes, which makes it hard to integrate them with existing hardware, especially when there is not much space. For example camera-based tactile sensors need a lot of space, so it is a problem to incorporate them. Also, developing sensors with intricate electrical components that fit into tight spaces needs sophisticated manufacturing techniques and it costs a lot. So we need tactile sensing technologies that are less complex and that can adapt easily to different shapes, limited space and form factors.

Measuring physical interactions accurately is very important in many physical robotic tasks, like human-robot interaction, object grasping, and manipulation. Tactile sensing can be used to observe the state of the interaction in physical robot interactions. Then tactile predictive models can make a predictive controller possible, for example for slippage control or cluster manipulation, and this gives actions that are safer, more precise and more efficient in a wider range of physical interaction tasks. Soft tactile sensors are important for handling deformable objects and for robust manipulation. They have a soft, flexible sensing surface, and the deformation of this surface gives tactile information like normal/shear forces, contact location, contact surface texture, etc. To convert the membrane deformation to tactile information, soft tactile sensors use electronic methods (e.g., resistive, capacitive, piezoelectric, magnetic, impedance), non-electronic transduction methods (e.g., camera-based, fluid-based, and acoustics) and also combinations of them.

Zoller et al. proposed a simple idea for tactile sensing where sound waves are used in a pneumatically actuated soft finger. They put a speaker and a microphone inside the chamber of the finger that is used for the pneumatic actuation. The microphone keeps monitoring the changes in the sound modulation. If the finger deforms because of an external force, the amplitude of the sound waves changes. With this added sensing capability they used the finger to measure contact forces and contact location with a certain precision. But the sensor is integrated with a soft finger, it is not a stand-alone sensor that could be used on other robot counterparts.

4. Acoustic tactile sensors
- tactile features: contacts, deformations, forces, shape recognition
- Shinoda et al.: silicone hemispherical fingertip, ultrasound transmitter/receiver array; deformations up to 10µm, inclination changes to 0.001 radians; later hollow cavity, stress via acoustic resonance
- Teramoto et al.: flexible membrane over acoustic transducers, object curvature
- Tanaka et al.: real-time lump detection in laparoscopic surgery, silicone hollow tube
- Chuang et al.: ultrasonic, static normal force (1-6 N), shape recognition, time-of-flight; TFT layer between piezoelectric PVDF layers + soft polymer surface -> sophisticated manufacturing

5. Lessons + AST
- V. Wall et al.: force location + material characteristics, soft pneumatic finger, enclosed speaker + microphone ("revolution")
- microphone only: still forces, locations, materials, but needs sound generated at contact point
- potential of acoustics for soft deformation
- low-cost skin: (1) no complex circuitry in skin, (2) sensory hardware away from surface -> compact, no sophisticated manufacturing, many form factors
- AST: low-cost, easily manufacturable standalone sensor

6. Contributions
- stand-alone, low-cost, different shapes and sizes (Fig. 1 a)
- (i) open-source low-cost sensor, easy to fabricate; key parts: membrane with embedded acoustic channels, microphone, speakers
- (ii) frame-less AST (f-AST) for non-flat surfaces
- (iii) regression and classification methods: force + location vs microphone readings
- (iv) robotic tasks: flat and non-flat surface, force-controlled pick-and-place -> realistic applications

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Soft tactile sensing has made progress, but it still has persistent limitations, as a recent review on tactile sensing technologies discusses. A lot of the soft tactile sensors that are commercially available have fixed shapes and sizes, which makes it hard to integrate them with existing hardware, especially when there is not much space. For example camera-based tactile sensors need a lot of space, so it is a problem to incorporate them. Also, developing sensors with intricate electrical components that fit into tight spaces needs sophisticated manufacturing techniques and it costs a lot. So we need tactile sensing technologies that are less complex and that can adapt easily to different shapes, limited space and form factors.

Measuring physical interactions accurately is very important in many physical robotic tasks, like human-robot interaction, object grasping, and manipulation. Tactile sensing can be used to observe the state of the interaction in physical robot interactions. Then tactile predictive models can make a predictive controller possible, for example for slippage control or cluster manipulation, and this gives actions that are safer, more precise and more efficient in a wider range of physical interaction tasks. Soft tactile sensors are important for handling deformable objects and for robust manipulation. They have a soft, flexible sensing surface, and the deformation of this surface gives tactile information like normal/shear forces, contact location, contact surface texture, etc. To convert the membrane deformation to tactile information, soft tactile sensors use electronic methods (e.g., resistive, capacitive, piezoelectric, magnetic, impedance), non-electronic transduction methods (e.g., camera-based, fluid-based, and acoustics) and also combinations of them.

Zoller et al. proposed a simple idea for tactile sensing where sound waves are used in a pneumatically actuated soft finger. They put a speaker and a microphone inside the chamber of the finger that is used for the pneumatic actuation. The microphone keeps monitoring the changes in the sound modulation. If the finger deforms because of an external force, the amplitude of the sound waves changes. With this added sensing capability they used the finger to measure contact forces and contact location with a certain precision. But the sensor is integrated with a soft finger, it is not a stand-alone sensor that could be used on other robot counterparts.

Acoustic techniques have been looked at for getting tactile features like contacts, deformations, forces and shape recognition. For example, Shinoda et al. made a silicone hemispherical fingertip with an ultrasound transmitter and receiver array embedded in it, and it can detect deformations up to 10µm and inclination changes to 0.001 radians. Later they improved the design by adding a hollow cavity in the membrane so they could measure stress by acoustic resonance. Teramoto et al. introduced a flexible membrane with acoustic transducers under it to measure the curvature of an object when it makes contact. Tanaka et al. made an acoustic sensor for detecting lumps in real time in laparoscopic surgery, which uses a silicone-based hollow tube and analyses how the sound waves deform through the tube.

Chuang et al. designed an ultrasonic sensor that can measure static normal forces in real time (1-6 N) and also recognise shapes, by analysing the variations in time-of-flight of ultrasonic pulses that come from surface deformation. In the sensor there is a Thin Film Transistor layer between piezoelectric PVDF layers, and a soft polymer sensing surface. This design needs sophisticated manufacturing. A revolution was brought by V. Wall et al., who extended the acoustic methods to find the force location and material characteristics with a soft pneumatic finger that has an enclosed speaker and microphone. With only a microphone the design can still measure contact forces, locations and materials, but then sound has to be generated at the contact point for it to work. These reports show that there is potential in using acoustic techniques to get tactile information from the deformation of soft material. But if we want to develop a low-cost tactile sensing skin, it is better (1) not to put complex electronic circuitry into the skin, and (2) to move the sensory hardware away from the sensing surface, since this makes the sensor compact and avoids needing sophisticated manufacturing techniques. This also allows a lot of different skin form factors. We made AST as a standalone sensor that is low-cost and easy to manufacture.

In this paper we present a tactile sensing technology that is stand-alone and low-cost and can be used in different shapes and sizes, which we call Acoustic Soft Tactile skin (AST) (Fig. 1 a). Our contributions are: (i) a new open-source low-cost tactile sensor that is easy to fabricate to fit different shapes, where the only key components are a membrane with embedded acoustic channels, a microphone, and speakers. (ii) A design for a frame-less AST (f-AST) for surfaces that are not flat. (iii) We looked at different regression and classification methods to learn the relation between the applied force and its location and the microphone readings for our AST designs while we tested its performance. (iv) We show AST in robotic tasks where it is attached to a flat and a non-flat surface and does force-controlled robotic pick-and-place tasks. These tests show that the AST technology can be used in realistic robotic applications.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Despite advancements in soft tactile sensing, persistent limitations remain (as discussed in a recent review on tactile sensing technologies [1]). Many commercially available soft tactile sensors come with fixed shapes and sizes, which makes integration with existing hardware challenging, especially in space-constrained environments. For instance, incorporating camera-based tactile sensors is problematic because of their space requirements [2,3]. Furthermore, developing sensors with intricate electrical components that fit tight spaces demands sophisticated manufacturing techniques and incurs high costs. There is a need for less complex tactile sensing technologies that can easily adapt to various shapes, limited space and form factors.

Accurate measurement of physical interactions plays a vital role in various physical robotic tasks, such as human-robot interaction [4], object grasping, and manipulation [5]. Tactile sensing can be used to observe the interaction state in physical robot interactions [6]. Tactile predictive models [7] can then make a predictive controller possible, e.g. for slippage control [8] or cluster manipulation [9], leading to safer, more precise and more efficient actions in a broader range of physical interaction tasks [7,10,11]. Soft tactile sensors are important for handling deformable objects and for robust manipulation. These sensors feature a soft, flexible sensing surface whose deformation provides tactile information such as normal/shear forces, contact location, and contact surface texture, etc. Soft tactile sensors use both electronic (e.g., resistive [12], capacitive [13], piezoelectric [14], magnetic [15,16], impedance [17]) and non-electronic transduction methods (e.g., camera-based [18,19,2,20,21,22,23], fluid-based [24], and acoustics [25,26,27,28]) and their combinations [29] to convert the membrane deformation to tactile information.

Zoller et al. [31] proposed a simple concept for tactile sensing that applies sound waves to a pneumatically actuated soft finger. They added a speaker and a microphone within the finger's chamber for pneumatic actuation, and the microphone continuously monitors changes in sound modulation. If the finger deforms due to an applied external force, the amplitude of the sound waves changes. They used the finger with this added sensing capability to measure contact forces and contact location with a certain precision [32]. However, the sensor is integrated with a soft finger and is not a stand-alone sensor that can be used on other robot counterparts.

Acoustic techniques have been explored for deriving tactile features like contacts, deformations, forces, and shape recognition. For instance, Shinoda et al. [33] created a silicone hemispherical fingertip with an embedded ultrasound transmitter and receiver array, capable of detecting deformations up to 10µm and inclination changes to 0.001 radians. They later improved this design by adding a hollow cavity within the membrane to measure stress via acoustic resonance. Teramoto et al. [28] introduced a flexible membrane underlaid with acoustic transducers to measure object curvature upon contact. Tanaka et al. [27] devised an acoustic sensor for real-time lump detection in laparoscopic surgery, using a silicone-based hollow tube and analysing sound wave deformations through the tube.

Chuang et al. [25] designed an ultrasonic sensor capable of real-time static normal force measurements (1-6 N) and shape recognition, which analyzes time-of-flight variations in ultrasonic pulses caused by surface deformation. The sensor architecture includes a Thin Film Transistor layer sandwiched between piezoelectric PVDF layers and a soft polymer sensing surface, a design that calls for sophisticated manufacturing. However, a revolution was brought by V. Wall et al. [32], who extended acoustic methods to pinpoint the force location and material characteristics using a soft pneumatic finger with an enclosed speaker and microphone. With only a microphone, this design can still measure contact forces, locations, and materials, although it then requires sound generation at the contact point to function [34]. These reports show the potential of using acoustic techniques to extract tactile information from soft material deformation. But for developing a low-cost tactile sensing skin, it is advisable (1) not to integrate complex electronic circuitry into the skin, and (2) to relocate the sensory hardware away from the sensing surface, which enables sensor compactness and avoids sophisticated manufacturing techniques. This also allows for a variety of skin form factors. We made AST [35,36] a low-cost and easily manufacturable standalone sensor.

This paper presents a stand-alone and low-cost tactile sensing technology suitable for use in different shapes and sizes, called Acoustic Soft Tactile skin (AST) (Fig. 1 a). Our contributions include (i) a novel open-source low-cost tactile sensor that is easy to fabricate to fit different shapes; a membrane with embedded acoustic channels, a microphone, and speakers are its only key components. (ii) We also present a design for a frame-less AST (f-AST) for non-flat surfaces. (iii) We investigated different regression and classification methods for learning the relation between the applied force and its location and the microphone readings for our AST designs during performance testing. (iv) We demonstrate AST in robotic tasks where it is attached to a flat and a non-flat surface and performs force-controlled robotic pick-and-place tasks. These tests show that AST technology can be used in realistic robotic applications.
